title: Scalability
scopeHtml: Scope: what scaling means, vertical vs horizontal, stateless services, load balancing and the first bottlenecks.

notes.title: What scalability means
notes.html:
Scalability is how well a system keeps working when the load grows, without a rewrite. Load can be requests per second, users, data size or writes per second. A system is scalable if adding resources (money, machines) gives roughly proportional extra capacity.

It is not the same as "fast". A shop with one cashier can be fast for 5 customers and collapse at 500. Speed is latency; scalability is what happens to latency as load rises.

Worked example. 10M users, each opens the app 5 times a day: 50M requests/day, divided by 86,400 s is about 580 requests/s on average. Peak is usually 3x the average, so plan for about 1,700 requests/s. One well-tuned app server handles roughly 500 to 2,000 simple requests/s, so you need 2 to 4 servers plus spare for failures.

Industry examples. WhatsApp served hundreds of millions of users with very few engineers by keeping each Erlang server small and stateless-ish. Instagram started as one Django app on one machine and scaled by adding servers and caches, not by redesigning.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant that is full on Saturday: you can hire faster chefs, or open a second kitchen. Scalability is how painless it is to open that second kitchen.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "we will scale it" with no number. Always estimate the load first.
  • Mixing up latency and scalability.
  • Designing for 1B users on day one; that is over-engineering and costs money.

notes.title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
notes.html:
Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger machine: more CPU, RAM, faster disk. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means more machines behind a load balancer.

Vertical Horizontal
Effort Almost none, no code change Needs stateless code, a load balancer
Limit The biggest machine you can buy Practically none
Failure One machine = one big failure One of many fails, rest continue
Cost curve Gets steeply expensive at the top Roughly linear with commodity boxes

Why the decision matters (gravity). Vertical is the right first move: it is reversible, cheap in engineering time, and a single Postgres on 64 cores serves a surprising amount of traffic. Horizontal scaling of the database is a one-way door (sharding), so you delay it as long as is sensible. Stack Overflow famously ran on a handful of beefy SQL Server machines for years.

When it breaks. Vertical stops at the hardware ceiling and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal fails if the app keeps state in memory (see next section).

Everyday analogy. Buying a bigger truck versus buying more trucks. A bigger truck is simple until the biggest truck is not big enough, or breaks down and everything stops.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming horizontal is always better. At low scale vertical is simpler and cheaper.
  • Forgetting that scaling the stateless tier does nothing if the database is the bottleneck.

notes.title: Stateless servers
notes.html:
A stateless server keeps nothing about a user between requests. Any server can answer any request, because everything it needs comes with the request (a token) or sits in a shared store (database, Redis).

If server 1 keeps your login session in its own memory, a request that lands on server 2 sees a stranger. The fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Signed token (JWT or opaque ID plus shared store): the request carries or references the state.
  2. Shared session store: Redis holds sessions, all servers read it.
  3. Sticky sessions: the load balancer always sends a user to the same server. Easy, but it unbalances load and loses sessions when that server dies.

Config example (typical). Session TTL 30 min sliding, Redis with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru, 2 replicas. A session is about 1 KB, so 10M concurrent sessions need about 10 GB of RAM.

Industry examples. Netflix and Uber run their API services stateless so instances can be killed and replaced at any time (autoscaling, spot instances, deployments).

Everyday analogy. A bank where any teller can help you because your account is in the shared computer, not in the teller's head. If tellers memorised customers, you could only use one window.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting uploads on local disk of an app server; the next request lands elsewhere.
  • Using sticky sessions and then being surprised by a hot server after a deploy.

notes.title: Load balancing basics
notes.html:
A load balancer (LB) spreads incoming requests over a pool of servers and stops sending traffic to dead ones.

Choices that matter:

  • Layer 4 (TCP): fast and simple, only sees IPs and ports. Layer 7 (HTTP): reads URLs and headers, so it can route /api and /images differently, terminate TLS and do canary releases. Costs more CPU.
  • Algorithms: round robin (default, fine for equal requests), least connections (better when requests vary a lot), consistent hashing (same key to the same server, good for caches).
  • Health checks: for example HTTP GET /health every 5 s, mark unhealthy after 3 failures, healthy after 2 successes. Too aggressive and a slow moment drains the whole pool.

Industry examples. AWS ALB (L7) and NLB (L4), NGINX, HAProxy and Envoy. Google's Maglev and Facebook's Katran are software L4 balancers handling millions of packets/s.

Everyday analogy. The host at a restaurant door who sends each group to a table with room, and skips tables that are closed.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting that the LB itself is a single point of failure; real setups run LBs in pairs or behind DNS/anycast.
  • Round robin with long-lived connections (WebSockets): connection counts become uneven.

notes.title: Where scaling breaks next
notes.html:
Adding app servers moves the bottleneck. The usual order in which things hit the wall:

  1. App CPU: fixed by more servers (cheap).
  2. Database reads: fixed by indexes, then a cache, then read replicas.
  3. Database writes and size: fixed by vertical scaling, then partitioning/sharding (expensive, hard to undo).
  4. A single hot key or single region: fixed by splitting the key, replication and multi-region.

The skill the interviewer tests is naming the next bottleneck and the cheapest fix for it, with a number to justify it.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to sharding and microservices before measuring.
  • Not saying what you would measure (CPU, p99 latency, DB connections, replication lag).

notes.title: Describing the load before you scale
notes.html:
You cannot discuss scaling until you can say how busy the system is, in numbers. Three numbers do most of the job: requests per second at the peak (not the average), the read:write split, and the shape over time (steady, daily wave, or a spike on the calendar).

Worked example. 10M users a day, 50 requests each: 500M requests/day. Use 100,000 s/day for easy mental math: 5,000 req/s on average. A flash sale opens at noon and 2M people show up in 5 minutes, 30 requests each: 60M requests in 300 s, or 200,000 req/s, forty times the daily average. At 1,000 req/s per app server, the average day needs 5 servers and the sale needs 200. The hard part is the five minutes, not the day.

The read:write split decides the tools: shopping and browsing are 99% reads (cache, CDN, replicas), while payments and bookings are writes (queues, sharding, careful locking).

Industry examples. Ticketing and sale sites (IRCTC Tatkal, Flipkart Big Billion Days, Ticketmaster drops) plan around a known minute, not an average. Twitter's timeline is read-heavy by about 100:1, which is why it fans out on write.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant is sized for the Saturday 8 pm rush, not for the Tuesday afternoon average.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting averages when the system dies at the peak.
  • Not asking for the read:write ratio, which changes the design.
  • Giving "millions of users" with no requests per second.

notes.title: Calendar peaks: scale before the spike
notes.html:
When you know the peak is coming, add capacity before it, because autoscaling is late. Autoscaling reacts to a metric that has already crossed a threshold, then waits for servers to boot, load code, warm caches and pass health checks. That is 3 to 10 minutes, and a spike can be over, or have already knocked you over, in that time.

Tools, in the order you reach for them:

  1. Scheduled scale-out: raise the minimum fleet size at 11:45 for the noon sale and lower it afterwards.
  2. Pre-warm: fill caches and open connection pools before traffic arrives.
  3. Waiting room / virtual queue: admit users at a rate the backend can serve and show them their place in line, instead of letting everyone hammer the booking path at once.
  4. Hot-key fixes: one popular item (a single train, one phone model) becomes a hot key; split its counter across several keys or serve it from a cache.
  5. Load shedding and degradation: turn off recommendations and reviews so checkout stays up.

Industry examples. Ticketmaster and Cloudflare Waiting Room use virtual queues; Amazon pre-scales for Prime Day; IRCTC throttles and uses queues around the 10:00 Tatkal window.

Everyday analogy. A stadium opens extra gates and puts barriers in the street before the match, not after the crowd arrives.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "autoscaling" to a spike you can see on the calendar.
  • Scaling the web tier and forgetting the database connection limit.
  • Treating a waiting room as a failure instead of a deliberate throttle.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Scalability = staying healthy as load grows. Estimate load first (requests/s, peak 3x).
  • Scale up first (cheap, reversible); scale out when you hit limits or need availability.
  • Horizontal scaling needs stateless servers: state goes in tokens or a shared store.
  • A load balancer (L4 vs L7, round robin vs least connections, health checks) spreads traffic, and must itself not be a single point of failure.
  • Every fix moves the bottleneck: CPU, then DB reads, then DB writes, then hot keys, then regions. Name the next one.

questions.promptHtml: What does "scalable" mean, and how is it different from "fast"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates use the words interchangeably. A senior separates latency (one request) from scalability (behaviour as load grows).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Fast is latency for one request. Scalable means that when load grows, say 10x, I can keep latency and error rate healthy by adding resources, roughly in proportion, without a rewrite. A system can be fast at 5 users and collapse at 500; that is fast but not scalable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Load has several axes: requests per second, concurrent users, data size, writes per second. "Scalable" is always relative to one of them. The test is the curve of latency versus load and the cost per extra unit of load.

latency
  |            .  not scalable (queueing, saturation)
  |          .
  |  ______.______  scalable (flat, add servers to stay flat)
  +------------------ load (req/s)

Latency rises sharply once a resource saturates (queueing theory: wait time explodes as utilisation approaches 100%). So the useful question is "which resource saturates first, and what does it cost to add more of it".

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "we will scale it" with no number for current or target load.
  • Designing for 1B users on day one; that is over-engineering.
  • Measuring only average latency; saturation shows up at p99 first.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you quantify the load? -> Peak requests/s, read:write ratio, data growth per day.
  2. Is more throughput always more scalable? -> No; if cost per request grows with load (lock contention, N+1 fan-out) it is not.
  3. What is the first sign of saturation? -> p99 rising while CPU average still looks fine, queue depth growing, connection pool waits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "handles more users." Senior: defines the load axis, names the saturating resource, and ties scaling to proportional cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams optimise p50 by 20% and are surprised when a 3x traffic day still pages them, because the bottleneck was a connection pool, not code speed.

questions.promptHtml: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling. Which would you reach for first and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you default to buzzwords (always scale out) or reason about reversibility and cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Vertical means a bigger box, horizontal means more boxes. I go vertical first because it needs no code change, is reversible, and a single large Postgres serves a lot. I go horizontal for the stateless app tier early, because it also gives availability, and for the database only when a number forces me, since sharding is a one-way door.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Vertical Horizontal
Effort Resize Stateless code, LB
Limit Biggest machine Practically none
Failure One big blast radius Partial failure
Cost curve Steep at the top Roughly linear

Horizontal needs the app to hold no local state. For data stores, horizontal means partitioning, which changes keys, queries and transactions.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Horizontal is always better." At low scale it adds operational cost.
  • Scaling the web tier when the database is the bottleneck.
  • Ignoring that vertical leaves a single point of failure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is vertical enough? -> Writes of hundreds to low thousands per second and data in the low TBs, with replicas for reads.
  2. What is the gravity of each? -> Vertical reversible; DB sharding one-way door.
  3. How do you get availability on a vertical DB? -> Primary with a standby and automated failover, multi-AZ.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists the table. Senior adds reversibility, the DB-is-the-exception point, and the cost-curve crossover.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team sharded early "for scale", then spent a year on cross-shard joins for a dataset one 32-core node would have held.

questions.promptHtml: What makes a server stateless, and how do you handle user sessions when you need to scale out?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Statelessness is the precondition for horizontal scaling and safe deploys. Interviewers check you know the options and their costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Stateless means any server can serve any request because the state travels with the request or lives in a shared store. For sessions I prefer a signed token or an opaque ID backed by Redis; sticky sessions are a last resort because they unbalance load and lose sessions when the node dies.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client -> LB -> App A ---\
              -> App B ----> Redis (sessions, TTL 30 min sliding)

Options: (1) self-contained signed token (JWT): no lookup, but hard to revoke, size on every request; (2) opaque ID plus Redis: easy revoke, one extra hop (~0.5 ms); (3) sticky sessions: no shared store, but uneven load and session loss on deploy. Sizing: ~1 KB per session, 10M concurrent is ~10 GB RAM before replication. Other hidden state: uploads on local disk, in-process caches that must be consistent, scheduled jobs that run on every node.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saving uploads to the local disk of one app server.
  • JWT with no revocation story.
  • Redis single instance as a new single point of failure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you log a user out everywhere with JWT? -> Short expiry plus a denylist or session version check.
  2. What if Redis dies? -> Replicas with failover; degrade to re-login; do not take the app down.
  3. Is a local in-memory cache a violation? -> Not if it is a cache of shared truth with a short TTL and tolerated staleness.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use JWT." Senior: compares token vs store with revocation and sizing, and hunts for hidden state like disk and cron.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An upload feature worked on one node in staging and failed intermittently in production behind three nodes.

questions.promptHtml: How does a load balancer work? Cover L4 vs L7, algorithms and health checks.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The LB appears in every design. Weak candidates draw a box; strong ones know what it costs and how it fails.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LB spreads requests across a pool and skips dead servers. L4 routes by IP and port and is fast; L7 reads HTTP so it can route by path, terminate TLS and do canaries, at more CPU. Round robin suits uniform requests, least-connections suits variable ones, consistent hashing suits caches. Health checks need sane thresholds, and the LB itself must be redundant.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Health check example: GET /health every 5 s, unhealthy after 3 failures, healthy after 2 successes. Too aggressive and a GC pause drains the pool; too lax and users hit dead nodes for 30 s. The /health endpoint should be cheap and not depend on every downstream, else one dependency outage removes all nodes. Long-lived connections (WebSockets) make round robin uneven: connections stay, so count balances only at connect time; use least-connections and drain gracefully on deploy. LB redundancy: active-passive pair with a virtual IP, or multiple LBs behind DNS/anycast.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the LB is a SPOF.
  • Deep health checks that cascade.
  • Round robin for WebSockets.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. L4 or L7 for gRPC? -> L7 aware of HTTP/2 streams; an L4 pins one connection to one backend.
  2. How do you deploy without dropping requests? -> Connection draining, readiness vs liveness probes.
  3. Which algorithm for a cache tier? -> Consistent hashing to keep keys on the same node and limit reshuffling.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE names algorithms. Senior covers health-check design, connection draining, LB redundancy and the long-connection trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A health check that queried the DB made a DB blip mark every app node unhealthy, turning a 20 s blip into a 5 minute outage.

questions.contextHtml: A consumer app has 10M users who each open it 5 times a day, about 10 requests per open. Product wants a server count for launch. A simple API server in your stack handles roughly 1,000 req/s at 60% CPU. Peak is about 3x average. A teammate says "10M users, so 100 servers."
questions.promptHtml: How many app servers, and how do you defend the number?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Pulls a number from the air, or uses users instead of requests per second, ignores peak and failure headroom.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak shape (daily wave or spikes)? Read:write split? Any heavy endpoints? Target p99? Multi-AZ requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I do the arithmetic first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Users are not the unit; requests per second are.
  4. How I'd verify: 10M x 5 x 10 = 500M requests/day; 500M / 86,400 = ~5,800/s average; x3 peak = ~17,500/s. At 1,000/s per server that is ~18 servers; I add N+2 or 30% headroom and AZ spread: ~24 across 3 AZs, so losing an AZ leaves 16, which is just under peak, so go to 27-30.
  5. Root cause: n/a; the teammate counted users, not load.
  6. Fix: Start at ~24, autoscale on CPU or request rate, and load-test the 1,000/s assumption since it is my assumption.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard requests/s, p99 and saturation, review quarterly.
  8. Trade-offs: 100 servers is ~4x the cost for headroom nobody needs; the DB and cache tiers still need their own sizing, since the DB will bottleneck first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Peak is a flash sale at 40x average? -> Different problem: scheduled scale-out and a waiting room, see the calendar-peak section.
  • The endpoints are 5x heavier? -> Re-measure per-server throughput; do not reuse 1,000/s.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch was sized from user count at 3x the needed fleet; the real bottleneck was the database connection limit at 500, hit with only 12 app servers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: server count from users with no per-second math.
  • Hire: correct requests/s, peak factor, per-server assumption.
  • Strong hire: adds AZ-loss headroom, flags the assumption to load test, names the DB as the next bottleneck.

questions.contextHtml:
You run 6 app servers behind an L7 LB with cookie-based sticky sessions. After a rolling deploy at 14:00, the dashboard shows:

host   cpu   active_sessions
app-1  22%   1,900
app-2  25%   2,100
app-3  24%   1,850
app-4  91%   9,800
app-5  88%   9,400
app-6  23%   2,000

Users on app-4 and app-5 report 4 s page loads. Error rate is 0.4%, mostly timeouts. The deploy finished cleanly. Memory is normal everywhere.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what happened and how you fix it now and permanently.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames "traffic" or adds servers, never connecting the skew to stickiness and the restart order.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was deploy order 1 to 6? Is session TTL long? Is any user heavy (bot or partner API) pinned? Is the LB cookie TTL browser-session or fixed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shift LB to a mode that ignores affinity for new requests, or drain app-4/5 by setting them to draining so sessions re-pin elsewhere; accept re-login if sessions are local.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Restarted nodes lose their sessions, those users re-pin to whichever node is up at that moment (the early-restarted ones are pinned to the late survivors); a few heavy clients pinned; LB algorithm for new sessions is skewed.
  4. How I'd verify: Per-node request rate and distribution of top client IPs, LB logs grouped by cookie ID, deploy timeline vs session count curves.
  5. Root cause: Stickiness makes load a function of history. During the rolling restart, evicted users re-pinned to nodes still up, and pins never rebalance until sessions expire.
  6. Fix: Short term: drain and rebalance. Long term: externalise sessions to Redis or tokens so any node serves any request, and remove stickiness.
  7. Prevention: Alert on per-node load skew (max/mean above 1.5), test deploys in staging with load.
  8. Trade-offs: Redis adds ~0.5 ms and a dependency that needs replicas; I would not just add servers because the new ones receive only new sessions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Legacy app cannot be made stateless this quarter? -> Sticky with least-connections for new pins, short cookie TTL, and slow rolling deploys with drain.
  • WebSocket apps? -> Stickiness is natural; control it with connection limits per node.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A deploy-time skew repeated every release until sessions moved to Redis; the team had blamed the "noisy neighbour" cloud for a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds servers.
  • Hire: connects stickiness plus restart order to skew, drains.
  • Strong hire: removes state, adds skew alerting, covers legacy fallback.

questions.contextHtml:
Traffic doubled this week. You scaled the app tier from 8 to 16 servers. Latency got worse, not better.

app cpu avg: 18%       p99: 3.8 s (was 700 ms)
db primary: cpu 94%    connections 780 / 800 max
db slow log: SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE user_id=? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20
rows examined: 410,000 per query, 2,100 qps
replicas: 2 idle (reads go to primary)

An engineer proposes sharding the orders table.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees to shard or adds more app servers; never reads the evidence that the DB is the saturated resource and the query is unindexed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there an index on (user_id, created_at)? Pool size per app instance? Which queries dominate? Is replica lag acceptable for this read?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scale app back or cap pool size per instance so connections stop climbing (16 x 50 = 800 hits the limit); route this read to replicas.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing composite index (410K rows examined for 20); connection exhaustion from more app nodes; reads on primary; the red herring is app CPU at 18%.
  4. How I'd verify: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the query; pg_stat_activity and pg_stat_statements; replica lag.
  5. Root cause: The bottleneck moved to the DB. More app servers added more connections and concurrent heavy queries.
  6. Fix: Add index (user_id, created_at DESC), route reads to replicas, add a connection pooler (PgBouncer). A cache comes after that.
  7. Prevention: Alert on DB CPU, connections used/max, slow queries; load test before doubling the fleet.
  8. Trade-offs: Sharding would be a one-way door and would not fix a missing index; replicas add lag, so read-your-writes for a user's own just-placed order needs primary or a short pin.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Index builds lock the table? -> Build concurrently (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres) off-peak.
  • After the fix, 3x growth again? -> Cache hot reads, then consider partitioning by time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A doubled fleet took down a primary because every instance held a pool of 100; the fix was a pooler and a ceiling on total connections.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shards or scales app further.
  • Hire: identifies index and connections, uses replicas.
  • Strong hire: orders the bottleneck ladder, handles read-your-writes and the connection math.

questions.contextHtml: A retailer's flash sale opens at 12:00. Historical data: 2M users arrive within 5 minutes, about 30 requests each, 99% are reads of the product page; checkout is about 1% of requests. Normal day: 5,000 req/s. Autoscaling is set on CPU 60%, with servers taking 6 minutes to be in service. Last year the site fell over at 12:01.
questions.promptHtml: Design the plan for this year's sale.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn on autoscaling" and "use a CDN" with no math and no admission control.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is stock limited (hot key)? Is login required to view? What is acceptable behaviour at overload: queue or reject? Budget for pre-scaling?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable before; plan: peak load = 2M x 30 / 300 s = 200,000 req/s, 40x the daily average. Checkout writes ~2,000/s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Where it broke last year: autoscaling late (6 min), DB connections, hot stock row, cold caches.
  4. How I'd verify: Load test to 250K req/s in staging; replay last year's traffic shape; watch DB connection max.
  5. Root cause: Reacting to a spike that was on the calendar.
  6. Fix: Scheduled scale-out at 11:45; serve product pages from CDN/cache (99% reads become cheap); pre-warm caches and connection pools; split the hot stock counter across N keys; waiting room admitting, say, 3,000 checkouts per second the backend proves it can handle; degrade recommendations and reviews first.
  7. Prevention: Game day a week before; runbook with kill switches.
  8. Trade-offs: Waiting room costs conversion for impatient users but protects the revenue path; over-provisioning for 1 hour is cheap compared with an outage. I would not rely on autoscaling.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Bots flood at 12:00:00? -> Rate limit and token challenges at the waiting-room entrance.
  • 100 units of stock, 200K buyers? -> Reserve atomically (decrement in Redis or DB with a conditional update) and queue the rest.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sale survived only because a feature flag turned off personalised recommendations, cutting backend calls per page by 60%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: autoscaling only.
  • Hire: scheduled scale, CDN, queue.
  • Strong hire: numbers, hot-key handling, degradation ladder, rehearsal.

questions.contextHtml:
An outage review: at 03:12 a Redis hiccup lasting 20 s caused all 12 app servers to be removed from the LB at once, and the site returned 503 for 4 minutes. Config and handler:

health_check:
  path: /health
  interval: 2s
  timeout: 1s
  unhealthy_threshold: 1
  healthy_threshold: 5
Languages: Java · Kotlin
@GetMapping("/health")
public ResponseEntity<String> health() {
    redis.ping();          // throws if Redis is slow
    db.query("SELECT 1");
    return ResponseEntity.ok("ok");
}
@GetMapping("/health")
fun health(): ResponseEntity<String> {
    redis.ping()          // throws if Redis is slow
    db.query("SELECT 1")
    return ResponseEntity.ok("ok")
}

Languages: Java, Kotlin
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and what is the corrected design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says "make Redis more reliable" and misses that the health check amplified a partial failure into a total one.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the app work without Redis (degraded)? Is there a separate readiness and liveness? Is there a "panic" mode on the LB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Force the pool healthy or disable the health check temporarily; raise thresholds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Dependency checks in /health; threshold of 1 failure at 1 s timeout; healthy_threshold of 5 x 2 s keeps nodes out 10 s after recovery, all nodes flap together.
  4. How I'd verify: LB logs for the removal times, app logs showing /health timeouts, Redis latency graph.
  5. Root cause: A shared dependency in the health check makes every node fail simultaneously, so removing them cannot help; there is nowhere to route.
  6. Fix: Liveness checks the process only; readiness checks only what the node cannot work without; use 3 failures and 5 s timeout; configure the LB to keep serving when all nodes fail (fail open or minimum healthy percent).
  7. Prevention: Test health behaviour by injecting dependency latency in staging.
  8. Trade-offs: A shallow check may route to a node with a broken DB pool, so add a per-node error-rate based outlier ejection instead of a deep ping.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Redis really is required? -> Fail readiness but keep the LB fail-open and alert; removing all nodes is worse than errors.
  • Slow start after recovery? -> Use slow-start weighting to avoid a thundering herd.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Deep health checks were copied from a tutorial; one downstream blip removed the fleet three times in a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes only Redis.
  • Hire: separates liveness and readiness, fixes thresholds.
  • Strong hire: fail-open, outlier ejection, injection test.

questions.contextHtml:
After scaling from 1 to 4 pods, users report "my cart sometimes empties" and "I get logged out randomly". The code:

Languages: Java · Kotlin
@RestController
class CartController {
    private final Map<String, Cart> carts = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Long> lastSeen = new HashMap<>();

    @PostMapping("/cart/{userId}/add")
    Cart add(@PathVariable String userId, @RequestBody Item item) {
        Cart c = carts.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> new Cart());
        c.add(item);
        lastSeen.put(userId, System.currentTimeMillis());
        return c;
    }
}
@RestController
class CartController {
    private val carts = HashMap<String, Cart>()
    private val lastSeen = HashMap<String, Long>()

    @PostMapping("/cart/{userId}/add")
    fun add(@PathVariable userId: String, @RequestBody item: Item): Cart {
        val c = carts.getOrPut(userId) { Cart() }
        c.add(item)
        lastSeen[userId] = System.currentTimeMillis()
        return c
    }
}

Languages: Java, Kotlin
questions.promptHtml: List every problem that appears when this goes multi-instance, and how you would fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only that a HashMap is not thread-safe.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can cart data be lost? TTL needed? Does the cart need to survive deploys? Guests allowed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Turn on sticky sessions as a stopgap, knowing it only hides it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: State in process memory: each pod has its own cart view; lost on every restart and deploy; HashMap is not thread-safe under concurrent requests; unbounded growth is a memory leak; userId from the path is an authorisation hole (any user can edit another's cart).
  4. How I'd verify: Send two requests that land on different pods; check heap growth; try another user's ID.
  5. Root cause: Local state in a service that must be replaceable at any time.
  6. Fix: Store carts in Redis (hash per user, TTL 7 days) or the DB; derive userId from the authenticated token; make add an atomic operation; remove lastSeen map.
  7. Prevention: Code review rule: no mutable fields in controllers; run two replicas in staging always.
  8. Trade-offs: Redis adds a hop and a failure mode; a durable cart needs DB write-behind. I would not use sticky sessions long term.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two tabs add items simultaneously? -> Atomic list append or optimistic version, not read-modify-write.
  • Redis failure? -> Degrade to read-only cart rather than lose data silently.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shipped "temporary" in-memory cache caused refund tickets only after autoscaling was enabled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only thread safety.
  • Hire: spots shared-state and restart loss, moves to shared store.
  • Strong hire: also finds the auth hole, atomicity, memory leak.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B SaaS has one Postgres primary (16 cores, 128 GB, 3 TB data) at 40% CPU peak, growing 8% per month, ~1,500 write TPS, 12,000 read QPS. The CTO wants to "move to a sharded database now so we never worry again." The company has 15 engineers. Largest instance in your cloud offers 96 cores and 768 GB.
questions.promptHtml: Make the call and defend it, including reversibility.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either "shard now, it is future-proof" or "never shard", with no growth math.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Tenant size distribution? Hot tenants? Cross-tenant queries? RTO/RPO? Budget for migrations?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; headroom exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Growth compounding: 8% a month is 2.5x a year, so 40% CPU becomes saturated in about 10 months; reads can leave via replicas; instance can go up 4-6x vertically.
  4. How I'd verify: Load test at 3x; profile top queries; check table sizes and write amplification.
  5. Root cause: n/a. It is a timing decision.
  6. Fix: Plan: replicas for reads and caching now, vertical upgrade next, partition large tables, and choose a shard key (tenant_id) in the schema today so a later shard is a re-home, not a rewrite. Set a trigger: at 65% CPU peak or 6 TB, start sharding project.
  7. Prevention: Add tenant_id to every table and query, avoid cross-tenant joins.
  8. Trade-offs: Sharding now costs a year of complexity (cross-shard transactions, migrations, ops) and slows features; it is a one-way door. Waiting risks a rushed migration, which the trigger mitigates.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One tenant is 30% of load? -> Isolate that tenant to its own shard or instance.
  • Need 99.99%? -> Multi-AZ failover, tested; separate concern from sharding.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team that sharded at 500 GB spent more on tooling than the hardware upgrade would have cost; another waited too long and migrated under load at 90% CPU.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: absolute stance with no numbers.
  • Hire: growth math, vertical plus replicas first.
  • Strong hire: trigger thresholds, shard-ready schema, tenant isolation.

questions.contextHtml: The interviewer says: "Design a backend that scales to 100 million users." Nothing else. You have 45 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do in the first five minutes, and what numbers do you derive?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts drawing load balancers, Kafka and shards immediately.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the product do (the core action)? DAU versus registered? Requests per user per day? Read:write ratio? Peak shape (steady, evening wave, event spike)? Latency target and availability target? Regions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I restate: "100M registered, say 20% DAU, 50 requests per user per day, 95% reads, 3x evening peak, p99 under 300 ms, one region first. Correct?"
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Derived load: 20M x 50 = 1B requests/day, ~10K/s average at 100,000 s/day, ~30K/s peak, ~1,500 writes/s at 5% writes.
  4. How I'd verify: Ask the interviewer to correct assumptions; sanity check against per-node capacities (app 1K to 10K/s).
  5. Root cause: n/a. The risk is solving a different problem.
  6. Fix: Design: stateless tier of ~10-15 servers behind an L7 LB, cache for reads (95% hit leaves ~1.5K DB reads/s), one primary plus replicas, and then name the next bottleneck: write volume and data size, with a sharding trigger.
  7. Prevention: Write the assumptions on the board for reference.
  8. Trade-offs: I would not start with sharding or microservices; 100M users does not mean 100M concurrent requests.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• It is a chat app with persistent connections? -> Concurrent connections, not req/s, becomes the sizing unit.
  • Spiky events? -> Then calendar-peak planning dominates the average.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A candidate who spent minute two on "what is the peak" avoided a full redesign; the prompt's real constraint was a once-a-year event.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: boxes before questions.
  • Hire: scopes and derives requests per second.
  • Strong hire: derives peak, read:write, names next bottleneck and triggers.
